policies.summary: Texas has no state siting permit for wind, solar or storage plants; municipalities regulate land use through zoning, and counties have no general zoning power, so projects in unincorporated areas face little local land use review.

restrictions.description: Comprehensive health and safety review of AI data centers and battery energy storage systems. Active as of 2026-09-23. The Commissioners Court unanimously adopted the signed order on 2026-07-27 following the July 13, 2026 public hearing; KWHI (2026-07-28) independently confirms the unanimous vote and describes the order's scope (equipment-manufacturer audits, an Energy Development Zone siting study by the County Fire Marshal and County Engineer, and injunctive-relief enforcement authority). No fixed term applies; the order remains in effect, by its own terms, until the Commissioners Court (in consultation with the County Fire Marshal) determines the Comprehensive Health and Safety Review is complete. No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row). Legal basis: Order of Austin County, Texas, Regarding Battery Energy Storage Systems and Data Centers Health and Safety Review, adopted by the Commissioners Court on 2026-07-27 under Texas Health and Safety Code section 121.003 and Texas Local Government Code section 352.016, among other authorities. The signed, executed order was located directly on austincounty.com (distinct from the earlier unsigned draft). It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.

projects.description: Cypress Creek Renewables' Massey Energy Storage, a 100 megawatt battery energy storage system on approximately 15.46 acres at 2015 Massey Tompkins Road, Baytown, Texas. On August 14, 2025 Baytown City Council voted 7-0 to rezone about 10 acres of the site from Mixed Residential to General Commercial (Ordinance No. 16,206) and 7-0 to grant the special use permit (Ordinance No. 16,207). At the public hearings before the votes, a laborers' union representative raised safety concerns and said a ballot signature drive would be started if required, and speakers for the Texas Climate Jobs Project and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers asked for a delay. A July 3, 2025 letter from Laborers International Union Local 350, IBEW Local 527 and the Texas Climate Jobs Project had urged the city to postpone consideration of the permit over safety concerns. The conditions recommended by staff and the Planning and Zoning Commission, and set out in the draft ordinance, require battery containers at least 200 feet from residential uses and 100 feet from other uses, a masonry wall at least 6 feet tall, and bufferyard "B" from ULDC Table 3.43-2 next to commercial districts and bufferyard "C" next to residential districts.

Balanced Rock Power's 400-megawatt Claire Battery Energy Storage Project on approximately nine acres at the corner of Bob Smith Road and Walker Road (1010 Bob Smith Road), Baytown, Texas, beside an existing CenterPoint Energy substation. Baytown City Council granted the special use permit 4-3 on November 13, 2025 (Ordinance No. 16,297) after a public hearing. Speakers argued for and against the project; opponents cited the site's closeness to homes, thermal runaway, insurance exclusions for lithium-ion battery fires and future ownership, and council members noted that community input was nearly evenly split.
John Greer, a Dallas oil investor with a family ranch in Clay County, spearheaded a multiyear fight against the proposed 100-MW Bluegrove wind project.
projects.long_description: John Greer, a Dallas oil investor with a family ranch in Clay County, spearheaded a multiyear fight against the proposed 100-MW Bluegrove wind project. Greer helped co-found Clay County Against Wind Farms, which held informational sessions against wind energy in Henrietta, Texas. One meeting sought to recruit the support of fighter pilots stationed at a nearby air force base by focusing on potential interference with radar systems. In June 2018, under pressure from residents and politicians, Innergex Renewable Energy Inc. formally canceled the project.

projects.description: In June 2005, a local resident group called Protect Our West Texas Landscape (POWTL) sued developer FPL Energy to prevent the construction of the 735.5-MW Horse Hollow Wind Energy Center.
projects.long_description: In June 2005, a local resident group called Protect Our West Texas Landscape (POWTL) sued developer FPL Energy to prevent the construction of the 735.5-MW Horse Hollow Wind Energy Center. POWTL alleged that the wind farm would drastically disrupt the local scenery. The court ruled that no law in Texas regulates aesthetics, prompting the plaintiffs to amend the complaint to assert public and private nuisance claims and to seek injunctive relief. In December 2006, a trial jury found against the plaintiffs. The case was dismissed, and the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2008, the Court of Appeals affirmed the judgment of the trial court on all respects except for the allocation of costs and remanded for further determination. While that appeal was pending, the same plaintiffs sued the Taylor County Commissioners, alleging that the tax abatements given to the wind farms in the area were unlawful; that lawsuit, however, was withdrawn within a couple of months for procedural reasons. The Horse Hollow Center has been operational since its commissioning in 2005.

projects.description: Apex Clean Energy proposed a 250-MW wind farm within a 50,000-acre area north of Schulenburg.
projects.long_description: Apex Clean Energy proposed a 250-MW wind farm within a 50,000-acre area north of Schulenburg. The development would include between 40 to 80 turbines, some up to 600 feet tall. Local opponents organized a Facebook page called “Fayette County Texas – Stop The Wind Turbines” and an opposition group called “FayCoSaysNo.” The groups were active at town hall meetings and recruited hundreds of residents to join in opposition. In June 2024, the County Commissioners held a public meeting at which over 140 local residents attended, with 10 speaking in opposition and none speaking in support. The leader of the opposition raised questions about fire safety, negative impacts on livestock and wildlife, and plans for disposal of the turbines. She also raised concerns with red flashing lights, humming sounds and moving shadows from the turbines. On August 8, 2024, the Fayette County Commissioners Court signed a non-binding resolution opposing commercial wind energy development. In October 2024, the developer issued a statement stating that “Fayette County is not a focus at the moment.”

A group called Callahan County Land Owners Against Wind Turbines issued a statement online claiming that developers would be digging into and potentially damaging local aquifers. As of March 2023, the 267-MW wind project and 87-MWdc battery storage system is under construction.

projects.description: In 2022, Pine Gate Renewables proposed a 123-MW solar farm on privately-owned land, which was projected to generate over $20 million in tax revenue for the county.
projects.long_description: In 2022, Pine Gate Renewables proposed a 123-MW solar farm on privately-owned land, which was projected to generate over $20 million in tax revenue for the county. In October 2023, opposing landowners filed a lawsuit in state court alleging environmental damage and contamination on their nearby properties and seeking a temporary restraining order to halt construction. In December 2023, the trial court issued a temporary restraining order pausing several components of the project. In February 2024, the court issued an order temporarily enjoining the developer from clearing trees and preparing the leased land unless the developer complied with specific requirements including developing a stormwater pollution prevention plan and obtaining construction permits approved by the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. Several disputes over potential violations of the injunction followed. In September 2024, a federal court again temporarily enjoined construction, but construction subsequently resumed.

projects.long_description: In October 2022, the Elgin Independent School District voted unanimously to reject an application for a 3,000-acre solar farm from Solar Proponent LLC. A local group called Friends of the Land had opposed the project, expressing concern that clearing the land of trees could exacerbate flooding and threaten wildlife.

projects.description: Enel Green Power proposed a 210-MW solar farm with a 70-MW battery energy storage site to be developed on approximately 2,350 acres.
projects.long_description: Enel Green Power proposed a 210-MW solar farm with a 70-MW battery energy storage site to be developed on approximately 2,350 acres. The project has faced significant local opposition. More than 1,100 residents signed a petition against any solar projects in the county. Opponents created the website “Citizens for Reasonable Regulation of Renewable Energy” to host blogs and campaigns against solar development in the county. The county commissioners voted to impose a countywide 180-day moratorium on commercial solar development, which was later rescinded, as there were questions as to the county’s authority to adopt and enforce it. At a local school board meeting held on October 6, 2022 to decide whether to provide tax credits to the developer, opponents of the project voiced concerns over fire safety as well as water and soil contamination. In November 2022, although the school board rejected the tax credits, the developer proceeded with the project. In June 2023, two landowners filed a lawsuit in the County District Court seeking an injunction to stop the project. In July 2023, the defendants removed the case to the Texas Federal District Court, and the plaintiffs moved to remand. In March 2024, the Texas Federal District Court denied the motion to remand, dismissed the claims against one defendant, and allowed the remaining claims to be heard in federal court. In December 2025, the Texas Federal District Court granted the plaintiffs’ unopposed motion to dismiss without prejudice.

projects.description: The Wind Catcher Energy Connection Project was an interstate energy generation and transmission project that would have involved the construction of a 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle and hundreds of miles of interstate transmission lines into Texas and three other states.
projects.long_description: The Wind Catcher Energy Connection Project was an interstate energy generation and transmission project that would have involved the construction of a 2,000-MW wind farm in the Oklahoma panhandle and hundreds of miles of interstate transmission lines into Texas and three other states. In June 2018, the developer canceled the project after the Texas PUC denied a permit. Texas Industrial Energy Consumers—a trade association whose members included Chevron Phillips Chemical Company, ExxonMobil, and Valero Energy—had challenged the project before the PUC.

projects.description: The Lane City Wind Project is a 203-MW wind energy facility with approximately 59 wind turbines on 14,000 acres of land in Wharton County.
projects.long_description: The Lane City Wind Project is a 203-MW wind energy facility with approximately 59 wind turbines on 14,000 acres of land in Wharton County. Construction of the project began in the summer of 2024. In February 2025, a local ranch, Blue Creek Real Properties, sued the Department of Treasury and the developer, Lane City Wind, LLC seeking to halt construction and permanently block federal funding for the project. The lawsuit, filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas, alleges violations of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) due to potential risk to protected birds, including the Bald Eagle and Whooping Crane. In April 2025, the district court denied the defendant developer’s motion to dismiss the case and granted the joint motion to stay proceedings for 60 days. The district court has continued extending the stay, most recently until March 31, 2026.

projects.description: In 2023, OCI Energy proposed the 200-MW Lazy U Solar 1 facility to be located on farmland.
projects.long_description: In 2023, OCI Energy proposed the 200-MW Lazy U Solar 1 facility to be located on farmland. The project has faced local opposition by residents who have voiced concerns over tax subsidies, threats to protected wildlife, and the decommissioning of solar panels. In November 2025, Hardeman County officials approved a tax abatement for the project following a public meeting, despite the voiced opposition. The developer is in the process of relocating protected wildlife from the project site.

projects.description: In 2025, Xcel Energy proposed the 254-MW Oneida 2 Solar project to be located on approximately 1,300 acres in the Rolling Hills neighborhood, north of Amarillo in Potter County.
projects.long_description: In 2025, Xcel Energy proposed the 254-MW Oneida 2 Solar project to be located on approximately 1,300 acres in the Rolling Hills neighborhood, north of Amarillo in Potter County. In October 2025, Xcel Energy officially withdrew the proposal after more than 60 complaints were filed with the Texas Public Utility Commission and following a heated community meeting during which opponents of the project raised concerns about flooding, noise, wildlife displacement, and property values.

projects.description: In 2022, Savion Energy proposed the Buffalo Meadow Energy Center with 200 MW of solar energy generation and 150 MW of battery energy storage, to be constructed within the Franklin Independent School District in Robertson County.
projects.long_description: In 2022, Savion Energy proposed the Buffalo Meadow Energy Center with 200 MW of solar energy generation and 150 MW of battery energy storage, to be constructed within the Franklin Independent School District in Robertson County. In December 2022, the Franklin Board of Trustees approved the Agreement for an Appraised Value Limitation on Qualified Property requested by the developer. In March 2026, the Robertson County Commissioners held a public hearing at the county courthouse to discuss a tax abatement agreement for the project. Local residents packed the room and largely opposed the project, raising concerns about potential impacts on property values, water resources pollution, and fire safety.
